newsitem.title: USA: US July industrial output points to healthy growth.
newsitem.headline: US July industrial output points to healthy growth.

text.p: A modest rise in U.S. industrial production in July coupled with a drop in capacity utilization painted a picture of healthy third quarter growth devoid of worrisome inflation pressures, economists said.
Declining capacity use came despite a surge in utility production in the warm month, making the number all the more sanguine for economic health, they said.
"It's still very consistent with good growth in manufacturing and that's very favorable for the long-term outlook on the economy," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons."

The Federal Reserve said industrial production rose 0.2 percent in July from an unrevised 0.3 percent rise in June, while the rate of capacity utilization fell to 83.1 percent from a downwardly revised 83.3 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, that industrial production rose 0.2 percent in July. Capacity use was expected to come in flat at 83.5 percent.

Thayer said the data was largely in tune with the U.S. employment report for July, in which manufacturing payrolls fell by 5,000, while average weekly manufacturing hours worked per week fell to 41.7 from 41.8.
Some economists had expected the surprising strength in July's National Association of Purchasing Management's report to be reflected in the industrial output data.
But depressed by the General Motors Corp strike and various summer shutdowns, the number probably failed to capture the full potential of the economy, experts said.
"The GM strike took 0.1 percent from the overall number," said Jonathan Basile, economist at HSBC Markets, who added that industrial production numbers have been affected by auto strikes since April.
"Watch out for a rebound starting in August," Basile said.
Basile said the slide in the capacity utilization rate was important for financial markets "because we know that the Fed's focus earlier this year was on growth."
The reading is far from levels historically seen as provoking inflation, economists said.
Lower capacity use stems from a payback from strong capital spending seen this year, Thayer said.

"Throughout a lot of this economic expansion we've seen businesses willing to expand and become more productive," Thayer said. "It's a sign that this is still an expansion led by production and productivity."

Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A., also noted the divergence between purchasing managers' and government assessments of the manufacturing sector. But it is evident that capacity use is under less pressure now than the first four months of the year, Bhagavatula said.
One sector where capacity utilization remained high at a reading of 91.0 percent was primary metals.

"That's at the beginning of the production chain. Any kind of pick-up there may lead to higher activity down the road and would confirm the strong NAPM production, the highest in about 10 years. That was pretty alarming," Basile said.
